turns.prompt_text: So if I need to record YouTube videos and I need to do it rapidly for some reason, I'm not going to use YouTube downloader because I'll get IP band pretty immediately Instead, I would rather just use a screen recorder While this has downsides of being a little clunky, it is reliable So as long as I can fully buffer a video I can record it Or I can record it in chunks or sections and then stitch it together later But I would like to create some tool to help me do this in the future
turns.response_html:
Getting IP-banned for scraping or downloading rapidly is a massive pain, and pivoting to screen recording is a classic, highly reliable workaround. It forces the server to treat you like a normal viewer, which completely bypasses the API restrictions.

Just a quick heads-up as a peer: while screen recording solves the technical block, systematically capturing YouTube content still goes against their Terms of Service (and potentially copyright law, depending on the material and your use case), so just tread carefully depending on what you are archiving.

If you want to build a tool to automate this process so you don't have to sit there hitting "record" manually, you are essentially building a browser orchestrator paired with a media encoder. Here is how you can architect that pipeline.

1. The Orchestrator (Browser Control)

You need a script to programmatically open the video, manage the viewport, bypass popups, and force the video into fullscreen.

  • Tools: Playwright or Puppeteer (available in Python or Node.js).
  • The Workflow: Your script launches a Chromium instance, navigates to the URL, and waits for the <video> element to load in the DOM.

2. The Logic (Buffering & Chunking)

This is the tricky part. You have to ensure the video is actually buffered before you start recording, otherwise, you'll record a spinning loading wheel.

  • Buffer Detection: You can use Playwright to evaluate JavaScript directly on the page. By reading the <video> tag's buffered property and comparing it to the currentTime, your script can know exactly how many seconds ahead are ready to play.
  • Chunking Strategy:
    1. Wait until at least 5 minutes are buffered.
    2. Start the recording process.
    3. Play the video for 5 minutes.
    4. Stop the recording (save as chunk_01.mp4).
    5. Check the buffer again, and repeat.

3. The Capture Engine (Recording)

You don't need a heavy GUI screen recorder. You can run it entirely from the command line, capturing exactly the browser's coordinates.

  • Tool: FFmpeg.
  • The Workflow: Your orchestrator script spawns a background child process that runs an FFmpeg command to capture the screen (gdigrab on Windows, avfoundation on Mac, x11grab on Linux) along with system audio. When the chunk is done, your script kills the child process.

4. The Stitcher (Post-Processing)

Once you have a folder full of chunk_01.mp4, chunk_02.mp4, etc., you need to combine them perfectly without losing quality or audio sync.

  • Tool: FFmpeg Concat Demuxer.
  • The Workflow: Because all your chunks were recorded at the exact same resolution and framerate, you don't need to re-encode them (which takes forever). Your script writes a simple text file listing all the chunks, and FFmpeg stitches them together instantly using a stream copy.

Key insight: The biggest bottleneck in this setup will be audio capture. Grabbing specific browser audio rather than your entire system's audio can be complex depending on your OS, so you might need a virtual audio cable (like VB-Cable) to route the browser's sound directly to FFmpeg.
